## Introduction

In this project we build on our exploratory analysis from Project 2 of the 'Banking Dataset - Marketing Targets' from Kaggle. The data come from a Portuguese bank's marketing campaign, in which clients were called and offered a term deposit. We define our response variable as `y`, which is whether the client subscribed to the term deposit (`yes` or `no`). Since `y` is categorical, this is a classification problem.

Our goal is to predict whether a client will subscribe. Using the tidymodels framework, we fit a classification tree and a random forest. Each model is tuned with 5-fold cross-validation on a training set. We then compare the best version of each on a test set, and fit the winner to the entire data set. The API uses this final model to make predictions.

We use six predictors; three numeric and three categorical. These are the following:

- `age`: client's age (years)
- `balance`: client's average yearly account balance (euros)
- `campaign`: the number of contacts made with the client during this campaign
- `housing`: if the client has a housing loan
- `contact`: method of contact (`cellular`, `telephone`, or `unknown`)
- `poutcome`: prior outcome of previous campaign (`success`, `failure`, `other`, or `unknown`)

These predictors were chosen because they describe the client and their history with the bank, as well as findings from Project 2. Clients who were contacted in a previous campaign were more likely to subscribe, and subscribers tended to have higher balances and fewer contacts. 

We do not include `duration`, or the length of the last call. While `duration` was strongly related to subscription in Project 2, this information doesn't aid in prediction because it's only known after the fact. We also exclude `month`, or the month of the last contact. Despite observing monthly patterns in Project 2, there are many potential confounding variables not analyzed that could inhibit future predictions.

## Data

We begin by reading in the data. In Project 2 we found that `test.csv` was a duplicate subset of `train.csv`, so here we use only `train.csv`, which contains all 45,211 unique clients. We keep only our response and six chosen predictors, and convert the character columns to factors so the models treat them as categories.

```{r}
#| message: false
library(tidyverse)
library(tidymodels)

bank <- read_delim("data/train.csv", delim = ";") |>
  select(y, age, balance, campaign, housing, contact, poutcome) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.character), as.factor))
bank
```

```{r}
# Subscription counts
bank |>
  count(y) |>
  mutate(pct = round(100 * n / sum(n), 1))
```

Response is not balanced. Relevant for choosing metric and splitting data.

```{r}
# Split data 70/30, keeping same proportion of "yes" in each set
set.seed(558)
bank_split <- initial_split(bank, prop = 0.7, strata = y)
bank_train <- training(bank_split)
bank_test <- testing(bank_split)
bank_split

# 5 CV folds from training data
bank_folds <- vfold_cv(bank_train, v = 5)
```

```{r}
# Recipe: y predicted by all 6 predictors
bank_rec <- recipe(y ~ ., data = bank_train)
bank_rec
```

```{r}
# Metrics to evaluate models: log loss and accuracy
bank_metrics <- metric_set(mn_log_loss, accuracy)
```

`cost_complexity` controls how much the tree gets pruned. It penalizes trees for having more leaves.  

```{r}
# Classification tree model; only tune cost-complexity parameter
tree_mod <- decision_tree(cost_complexity = tune()) |>
    set_engine("rpart") |>
    set_mode("classification")

# Combine recipe and model into workflow
tree_wkf <- workflow() |>
    add_recipe(bank_rec) |>
    add_model(tree_mod)

# Tuning grid
tree_grid <- grid_regular(cost_complexity(), levels = 10)
```


```{r}
# Fit each grid value to the 5 CV folds
tree_fits <- tree_wkf |>
  tune_grid(resamples = bank_folds,
            grid = tree_grid,
            metrics = bank_metrics)

# CV log loss for each value (best first)
tree_fits |>
  collect_metrics() |>
  filter(.metric == "mn_log_loss") |>
  arrange(mean)
```

```{r}
# Best cost_complexity value by log loss
tree_best_params <- select_best(tree_fits, metric = "mn_log_loss")
tree_best_params

# Lock that value into the workflow
tree_final_wkf <- tree_wkf |>
  finalize_workflow(tree_best_params)
```

Random Forest

```{r}
# Random forest model; tune mtry
rf_mod <- rand_forest(mtry = tune()) |>
  set_engine("ranger") |>
  set_mode("classification")

# Combine recipe and model into workflow
rf_wkf <- workflow() |>
  add_recipe(bank_rec) |>
  add_model(rf_mod)

# Tuning grid: try every mtry value
rf_grid <- grid_regular(mtry(range = c(1, 6)), levels = 6)
rf_grid
```

```{r}
#| cache: true
# Fit each grid value to the 5 CV folds
set.seed(558)
rf_fits <- rf_wkf |>
  tune_grid(resamples = bank_folds,
            grid = rf_grid,
            metrics = bank_metrics)

# CV log loss for each value (listing best first)
rf_fits |>
  collect_metrics() |>
  filter(.metric == "mn_log_loss") |>
  arrange(mean)
```

```{r}
# Best mtry value by log loss
rf_best_params <- select_best(rf_fits, metric = "mn_log_loss")
rf_best_params

# Use best for workflow
rf_final_wkf <- rf_wkf |>
  finalize_workflow(rf_best_params)
```

Best is mtry = 2 with log loss approximately 0.311, which surpasses baseline and best tree. 


```{r}
# Fit best tree to full training set and evaluate on test set
tree_final_fit <- tree_final_wkf |>
  last_fit(bank_split, metrics = bank_metrics)
tree_final_fit |>
  collect_metrics()
```

```{r}
# Plot final tree
tree_final_fit |>
  extract_workflow() |>
  extract_fit_engine() |>
  rpart.plot::rpart.plot(roundint = FALSE)
```

```{r}
#| cache: true
# Fit best random forest to full training set and evaluate on test set
set.seed(558)
rf_final_fit <- rf_final_wkf |>
  last_fit(bank_split, metrics = bank_metrics)
rf_final_fit |>
  collect_metrics()
```

```{r}
# Compare both models on test set
rbind(tree_final_fit |> collect_metrics(),
      rf_final_fit |> collect_metrics()) |>
  mutate(Model = c("Tree", "Tree", "Random Forest", "Random Forest")) |>
  select(Model, everything())
```

Random forest is winner.

```{r}
#| cache: true
# Fit random forest to the entire data set
set.seed(558)
bank_final_model <- rf_final_wkf |>
  fit(bank)
bank_final_model
```
